title: The Deliverability Checklist: 4 Checks Before You Send a Single Cold Email
description: Not a copy problem, a deliverability problem. The 4 pre-send checks (domain, records, warm-up, inboxes) plus Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook rules in one table.
lead: This is the full deliverability checklist from the reel. You get a quick test to see if your problem is copy or deliverability, the 4 checks to pass before a single send (domain, records, warm-up, inboxes), how to test each one in minutes, and the Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook sender rules side by side, straight from their official pages.
insider: We run these 4 checks on every domain and inbox before a client campaign sends its first email. That's how our 5-day blitz sent **96,408 emails in five days with a 0.45% bounce rate** and booked 25 calls that same week: the inboxes were warmed up and checked before day one. The tactic is the easy part; the full system (list, inboxes, follow-ups) is what we do for clients.

blocks.text: Copy problem or deliverability problem?

If your best email and your follow-up both land in spam, nobody reads them. Rewriting the copy changes nothing, because the problem happens before anyone sees a single word. So before you touch the copy, find out which problem you have.

Don't use open rates to decide. [Google's sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126) say Google doesn't track open rates and that **low open rates aren't necessarily an accurate sign** of a spam problem. Use the signs below instead.

head: What you see
Most likely
Check first
rows: 0 replies of any kind. Not even out-of-office or "remove me" replies.
Send a test to your own Gmail and Outlook (Check 2 below)
Replies come in, but they're all "no thanks" or "not interested"
Your offer and who you email, not your setup
Pause and test that inbox before you send more
Verify the list before you send again
Results were fine, then dropped after you sent more per day
Check 4: spread volume over more inboxes
Your test email lands in Promotions or Spam

blocks.text: "If you want to know whether you're actually inboxing, watch your out-of-office replies. When those drop, you're going to spam, usually 48 to 72 hours before it fully tanks." (Quoted in [Hunter, State of Email Outreach 2026](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email))

[Hunter's report](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email) also found a **3.6% average bounce rate** and warns that above **2%** you're damaging your domain. A bad list is a deliverability problem too, so verify every list before it goes in.
The 4 checks on one card
Run these in order. If any check fails, don't send. One failed check can send every email to spam, no matter how good the copy is.

head: Check
Pass when
If it fails
rows: You send from a separate domain that looks like your brand, never your main domain or @gmail.com
SPF, DKIM and DMARC all show PASS on a test email
Fix the missing record, test again
Every inbox has at least 14 days of warm-up with zero cold emails
Your daily goal ÷ 30 = the number of inboxes you have (or more)
Add inboxes, don't push one inbox harder

blocks.text: Check 1: Domain

**Why it works:** your domain is your name tag. A free address looks like anyone could have sent it, and you can't set up your own records on it. In [Hunter's study of 31 million emails](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email), emails from a custom domain got **5.2% replies vs 2.5% from free addresses**. A separate sending domain also protects your main domain. If the sending domain gets a bad reputation, your client emails and invoices still arrive.

items: Buy a domain close to your brand. For acme.com, try getacme.com or acmehq.com. Stick to .com where you can.
Point the new domain to your real website, so anyone who types it in lands somewhere real.
Create your inboxes with a real email provider (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365), using real names like jane@getacme.com.
Never send cold email from your main domain. Keep that one for clients, invoices and normal mail.

blocks.text: Full domain setup, step by step: our [domain guide](/guides/domain.html).
Check 2: Records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)

**Why it works:** these three DNS records prove the email really came from you. [Google requires](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126) **SPF or DKIM from every sender**, and **SPF, DKIM and DMARC** from anyone sending more than 5,000 emails a day to Gmail. Google also recommends that you **always set up all three**, and says unauthenticated messages might be marked as spam or rejected. So treat it like the reel says: **one missing record means guilty until proven innocent.**

head: Record
Pass test
Detail that trips people up
rows: Only one SPF record per domain. It must list every service that sends for you.
Gmail needs a key of at least 1024 bits. Google recommends 2048 bits if your provider supports it ([Google DKIM help](https://support.google.com/a/answer/180504)).
Lives at _dmarc.yourdomain.com. Start with p=none, as [Google recommends](https://support.google.com/a/answer/2466580), and add rua= so you get reports.
The From: domain matches the SPF or DKIM domain
Required by Gmail and Yahoo for DMARC to pass. Sending through a tool on a different domain breaks it.

blocks.label: Starter DMARC record (TXT)
blocks.text:
Host / Name:  _dmarc
Type:         TXT
Value:        v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com

(Replace yourdomain.com with your sending domain. Make sure the dmarc@ inbox exists, or use any inbox you check.)

items: Run each sending domain through Google's free [Check MX tool](https://toolbox.googleapps.com/apps/checkmx/). Fix anything it flags.
Send a plain test email from each new inbox to a Gmail address you own.
In Gmail, open the email, click the three dots, then **Show original**. Look for **SPF: PASS**, **DKIM: PASS** and **DMARC: PASS**.

Do the same with an Outlook.com address. Microsoft explains how to [view message headers](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/view-internet-message-headers-in-outlook-cd039382-dc6e-4264-ac74-c048563d212c). Look for spf=pass, dkim=pass and dmarc=pass under Authentication-Results.
Any line that isn't PASS? Fix that record, wait for DNS to update, and test again. Exact values to paste are in our [DNS records guide](/blog/dns-records-for-cold-email.html).

blocks.label: One test per inbox
blocks.text: Test every inbox, not just one per domain. A typo in one inbox's setup only shows up when that inbox sends.
Check 3: Warm-up (14 days, no shortcuts)

**Why it works:** a brand-new inbox has no history. If its first act is 50 emails to strangers, it looks exactly like a spammer. Warm-up sends and receives normal-looking emails with other inboxes so providers learn you're real. [Instantly's warm-up guide](https://help.instantly.ai/articles/5975329-how-warm-up-works-and-why-it-s-important) says to **wait at least 2 weeks before using accounts for campaigns**, and [Instantly's 2026 benchmark report](https://instantly.ai/cold-email-benchmark-report-2026) says new domains need **4 to 6 weeks** of gradual increase to reach full volume.

Google says the same in its own words: [increase volume slowly](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126), send at a steady rate, and avoid sudden spikes. Google warns that suddenly doubling your volume could cause rate limiting or a reputation drop.

head: Days
Cold emails per inbox per day
Warm-up

blocks.text: Want it day by day? Our [30-day warm-up calendar](/guides/day30.html) lays it out.
Check 4: Inboxes (many, not one)

**Why it works:** each inbox and each domain builds its own reputation, and [Google tracks volume per domain and IP](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126). Google Workspace allows up to **2,000 emails a day** per user ([Google's limits page](https://support.google.com/a/answer/166852)), but that's a system limit, not a safe cold email number. In [Hunter's data](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email), accounts sending **20 to 49 emails a day got 5.7% replies vs 4.5% overall**. So keep each inbox at about 30 cold emails a day and add inboxes to grow.
Spreading out also limits the damage. If one domain gets a bad reputation, you pause 3 inboxes, not your whole operation. More detail in our [sending calculator](/guides/math.html).
Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook rules side by side

All three big inbox providers publish their sender rules. Here they are in one place, taken from each official page. The strictest rules are for big senders, but the same rules are what keep smaller senders out of spam, so follow them at any size.

head: Rule
Gmail
Yahoo
Outlook.com
rows: More than 5,000 emails a day to Gmail accounts
Domains sending more than 5,000 emails a day
SPF and DKIM, plus DMARC (p=none is fine), From: domain aligned
SPF and DKIM, plus DMARC of at least p=none that must pass, From: domain aligned
SPF must pass, DKIM must pass, DMARC at least p=none, aligned with SPF or DKIM
No number given. Keep lists clean
One-click unsubscribe for marketing messages, plus a visible link. Remove within 48 hours (recommended)
One-click unsubscribe for marketing messages, plus a visible link. Honor within 2 days
Easy, clearly visible way to opt out (recommended)
Spam folder or rejection. Since November 2025, Gmail is ramping up enforcement with temporary and permanent rejections

blocks.text: Sources: [Google sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126), [Google sender FAQ](https://support.google.com/a/answer/14229414), [Yahoo Sender Hub](https://senders.yahooinc.com/best-practices/), [Microsoft's Outlook announcement](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoftthreatprotectionblog/strengthening-email-ecosystem-outlook%E2%80%99s-new-requirements-for-high%E2%80%90volume-senders/4399730). Rules change, so check these pages every few months.

blocks.label: What your email provider handles
blocks.text: Forward and reverse DNS (PTR) and secure TLS connections are handled by Google Workspace and Microsoft 365. You mostly need to set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC yourself.
Worked example: 300 cold emails a day

items: **Inboxes:** 300 ÷ 30 = **10 inboxes**.
**Domains:** 10 ÷ 3 = 3.3, so round up to **4 domains** (3, 3, 2 and 2 inboxes).
**Records:** 4 domains × 3 records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) = **12 records** to add, then 10 test emails to Gmail and 10 to Outlook, one from each inbox.
**Warm-up:** days 1 to 14, zero cold emails. Use this time to build and verify your list.
**Ramp:** days 15 to 21: 10 inboxes × 10 = **100 a day**. Days 22 to 28: 10 × 20 = **200 a day**. Day 29 onward: 10 × 30 = **300 a day**.

**Spam rate check:** Google measures spam rate on mail that reaches Gmail inboxes. If 2,000 of your emails reach Gmail inboxes in a month, 0.1% is just **2 spam reports** and 0.3% is **6**. That's why the list and an easy opt-out matter so much.

The copy is never seen, so you can't learn anything from it
Run the 4 checks first, then test copy

blocks.text: Copy-paste prompt: run the pre-send check

blocks.label: Pre-send deliverability check
blocks.text:
Act as a cold email deliverability expert. Before I send a single email, check my setup against these 4 checks: domain, records, warm-up, inboxes.

My setup:
- Main business domain: [domain]
- Sending domains: [list]
- Email provider: [Google Workspace / Microsoft 365]
- Inboxes per domain: [number]
- For each domain, paste the SPF, DKIM and DMARC lines from a test email's headers (Gmail: Show original): [paste]
- Days of warm-up on each inbox so far: [number]
- Cold emails I plan to send per day in total: [number]
- Is my list verified? Bounce rate on last send: [yes/no, %]

For each check, say PASS or FAIL and why. For every FAIL, give the exact fix and tell me if I can send yet. Then tell me how many inboxes and domains I need at 30 cold emails per inbox per day and 3 inboxes per domain, rounding up. Be strict: if any check fails, the answer is "don't send yet".
The pre-send checklist

items: ☐ Sending from a separate domain, not my main domain and not @gmail.com
☐ Every inbox shows SPF: PASS, DKIM: PASS and DMARC: PASS on a test email
☐ DMARC record at _dmarc with p=none and a rua= address
☐ Every inbox has at least 14 days of warm-up and warm-up stays on
☐ Inboxes = daily goal ÷ 30, with no more than 3 inboxes per domain
☐ List verified, so bounces stay under 2%
☐ A plain opt-out line in every email, and opt-outs removed within 2 days
☐ [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com) set up for each sending domain
☐ Ramp plan written down: 10, then 20, then 30 a day per inbox

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.text: All boxes ticked? Send. One box empty? Fix it first. Skip these and your best email goes straight to spam.

faq.q: I send fewer than 5,000 emails a day. Do I still need DMARC?
faq.a: Gmail only requires SPF or DKIM below that number, but Google recommends always setting up SPF, DKIM and DMARC. It takes 5 minutes and removes one reason to land in spam. Set it up.

faq.q: Can I skip warm-up if my domain is a few years old?
faq.a: Don't send cold email from your main domain at all. A new inbox has no sending history even on an older domain, so give every new inbox at least 14 days of warm-up.

faq.q: How do I know if I'm in spam right now?
faq.a: Send a test from each inbox to your own Gmail and Outlook addresses, check [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com), and watch your out-of-office replies. If those suddenly drop, pause and test before you send more.

faq.q: Do cold emails need an unsubscribe link?
faq.a: Google's and Yahoo's one-click rules are written for marketing and subscribed messages from big senders. For cold email, at minimum give a plain way to opt out, like "Not the right person? Just reply and I won't email again," and remove people within 2 days.
